questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, plant growth regulators (PGRs) are best described as:

options.text: Large proteins that act only inside the cells that synthesise them
Small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition
Polysaccharides that all share one uniform chemical structure
Nucleic acids that are synthesised only at the root apex

solution.explanation: NCERT: the plant growth regulators are small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition. They can be indole compounds (IAA), adenine derivatives (kinetin), derivatives of carotenoids (abscisic acid), terpenes (gibberellic acid) or gases (ethylene). They are not large macromolecules and they are not all of one chemical type.
steps: Chemically diverse: indole compound, adenine derivative, carotenoid derivative, terpene, gas
solution.why_others_wrong: PGRs are not proteins, polysaccharides or nucleic acids, and they are of diverse (not uniform) chemical nature.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Growth and Development', plant growth regulators: characteristics
solution.final_answer: Option B: Small, simple molecules of diverse chemical composition

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: NCERT notes that because it regulates so many physiological processes, one plant growth regulator is one of the most widely used PGRs in agriculture. This PGR is:

options.text: Abscisic acid
Kinetin
Zeatin
Ethylene

solution.explanation: NCERT: since ethylene regulates so many physiological processes, it is one of the most widely used PGRs in agriculture. It is applied mostly as ethephon, which releases ethylene slowly inside the plant.

solution.why_others_wrong: Abscisic acid is described as a growth inhibitor and stress hormone; kinetin and zeatin are cytokinins. None of them is the PGR described in this NCERT line.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In plants, new cells are always being added to the plant body by the activity of the meristems. NCERT calls this form of growth:

options.text: The closed form of growth
Arithmetic growth
The open form of growth
Determinate growth

solution.explanation: Plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout their life because of meristems, whose cells can divide and self-perpetuate. NCERT: this form of growth, wherein new cells are always being added to the plant body by the activity of the meristem, is called the open form of growth.
steps: This is the open form of growth
solution.why_others_wrong: Closed or determinate growth stops at maturity, which is not the plant pattern; arithmetic growth is a type of growth rate (one daughter cell keeps dividing), not the name for this form of growth.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Growth and Development', growth: plant growth generally is indeterminate
solution.final_answer: Option C: The open form of growth

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: NCERT points out that the final structure of a cell at maturity is also determined by its location within the tissue. Which example does it give?

options.text: Cells positioned away from the root apical meristem mature as epidermis, while those pushed to the periphery differentiate as root-cap cells
Cells positioned away from the root apical meristem differentiate as root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis
Cells of the interfascicular region regain the capacity to divide and form interfascicular cambium
Leaves of buttercup produced in air differ in shape from those produced in water

solution.concept: Location of a cell decides its final structure
solution.explanation: NCERT: development in plants is open; cells and tissues arising from the same meristem have different structures at maturity, and the final structure is also determined by the location of the cell within the tissue. Example: cells positioned away from the root apical meristems differentiate as root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis.
steps: Away from the root apical meristem: root cap
solution.why_others_wrong: The first wrong option swaps the two fates. Interfascicular cambium formation is NCERT's example of dedifferentiation, and buttercup leaves are its example of heterophylly caused by the environment.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Growth and Development', differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation
solution.final_answer: Option B: Cells positioned away from the root apical meristem differentiate as root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery mature as epidermis

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Some plant responses are attributed in NCERT to more than one PGR. Which of the following statements are correct according to NCERT?

(a) Both gibberellins and cytokinins delay senescence.
(b) Both auxins and ethylene promote abscission (of older leaves and fruits, or of leaves and flowers).
(c) Both abscisic acid and gibberellins promote seed germination.
(d) Both cytokinins and auxins strengthen apical dominance.
(e) Both abscisic acid and ethylene can be regarded as largely inhibitors of growth activities.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (d) and (e) only
(a), (c) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (e) only

solution.explanation: (a) True: gibberellins delay senescence (fruits can be left on the tree longer) and cytokinins delay leaf senescence by nutrient mobilisation. (b) True: auxins promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits, and ethylene promotes senescence and abscission, especially of leaves and flowers. (c) False: abscisic acid inhibits seed germination. (d) False: auxins cause apical dominance, but cytokinins help to overcome it. (e) True: ABA is a general growth inhibitor, and NCERT says ethylene, though it fits either group, is largely an inhibitor of growth activities.
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with (c) or (d) is wrong; the option (a), (b), (c) leaves out (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Growth and Development', plant growth regulators: physiological effects
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (e) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In the same period, three leaves grow as follows: leaf P from 2 cm² to 3 cm², leaf Q from 10 cm² to 14 cm² and leaf R from 40 cm² to 46 cm². Which leaf has the highest absolute growth rate and which has the highest relative growth rate, respectively?

options.text: P and R
R and P
R and R
Q and P

solution.explanation: Absolute growth rate is the total growth per unit time: P = 1, Q = 4 and R = 6 cm², so R is highest. Relative growth rate is the growth per unit time expressed on a common basis, e.g. per unit initial parameter: P = 1/2 = 50%, Q = 4/10 = 40%, R = 6/40 = 15%, so P is highest.
steps: Absolute: P 1, Q 4, R 6 cm² → R highest
Relative: P 50%, Q 40%, R 15% → P highest
solution.shortcut: A small leaf with a modest gain can still have the highest relative growth rate.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'P and R' swaps the two rates; 'R and R' treats the relative rate like the absolute one; 'Q and P' picks the middle leaf for absolute growth.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Growth and Development', growth: growth rates
solution.final_answer: Option B: R and P

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A plant tissue grows geometrically according to W₁ = W₀e^(rt). Its mass rises from 3 g to 12 g in 10 days. Taking ln 2 = 0.693, what is its relative growth rate r, and what mass is expected at the end of 15 days if the same growth continues?

options.text: r ≈ 0.139 per day; 24 g
r ≈ 0.139 per day; 16.5 g
r = 0.4 per day; 24 g
r ≈ 0.139 per day; 48 g

solution.explanation: 12/3 = 4 = e^(10r), so 10r = ln 4 = 2 × 0.693 = 1.386 and r ≈ 0.1386 per day. Mass doubles every ln 2/r = 5 days; 15 days is three doublings, so W = 3 × 2³ = 24 g (equivalently 3 × e^(0.1386 × 15) = 3 × e^2.079 = 24 g).
solution.shortcut: Fourfold in 10 days means doubling every 5 days; 15 days = 2³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16.5 g extends the growth linearly (0.9 g per day), which is arithmetic, not geometric, growth; 0.4 per day divides the fold change by time instead of taking its logarithm; 48 g applies another fourfold increase to the 12 g mass in only 5 days.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Plant Growth and Development', growth: growth rates (geometric growth)
solution.final_answer: Option A: r ≈ 0.139 per day; 24 g

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which type of pollination is functionally cross-pollination because it involves a pollinating agent, but is genetically similar to autogamy because the pollen comes from the same plant?

Geitonogamy
Cleistogamy
Chasmogamy

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a mature two-celled pollen grain, the vegetative cell is:

options.text: Bigger than the generative cell, with abundant food reserve and a large, irregularly shaped nucleus
Smaller than the generative cell and spindle-shaped, floating in the cytoplasm of the generative cell
Bigger than the generative cell but without any nucleus
Equal in size to the generative cell, and divides to form the two male gametes

The generative cell is small and floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell; it is spindle-shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, and it is the generative cell that divides to give the two male gametes.

Which of the following are advantages of seeds to angiosperms, as given in NCERT?

(a) Since pollination and fertilisation are independent of water, seed formation is more dependable.
(b) Seeds have better adaptive strategies for dispersal to new habitats and help the species to colonise other areas.
(c) Seeds have sufficient food reserves, so young seedlings are nourished until they are capable of photosynthesis.
(d) The seed coat is thin and offers no protection to the young embryo.
(e) Mature seeds retain a high water content, which is crucial for their storage.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a species whose pollen grains are shed at the 3-celled stage, the pollen grain at the time of shedding contains:

options.text: One vegetative cell, one generative cell and one tube cell
Three male gametes
One generative cell and two vegetative cells
One vegetative cell and two male gametes

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Count every division of a single nucleus as one mitotic division event. Starting from (i) the functional megaspore of one ovule, which forms a typical mature embryo sac, and (ii) the four microspores formed from one pollen mother cell, each of which forms a pollen grain that produces two male gametes, how many mitotic division events take place in all?

solution.explanation: Embryo sac: the megaspore nucleus divides once (2 nuclei), then two more sequential free-nuclear divisions give 4 and then 8 nuclei; each round doubles the number of nuclei, so the events are 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. Pollen: each microspore nucleus divides once (vegetative + generative cell) and the generative cell divides once more (two male gametes): 2 events per microspore × 4 = 8. Total = 7 + 8 = 15.
solution.shortcut: Going from 1 nucleus to n nuclei by mitosis always takes n − 1 division events: 8 − 1 = 7; each microspore goes to 3 nuclei, 3 − 1 = 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 counts rounds of division (3) instead of events and only one pollen grain (2); 11 counts rounds for the embryo sac (3) but events for four pollen grains (8); 9 counts the embryo sac correctly but only one pollen grain.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation: megasporogenesis, female gametophyte and pollen grain
solution.final_answer: Option C: 15

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a Citrus seed, one embryo is zygotic and two others have developed from nucellar cells that protruded into the embryo sac. The nucellar embryos are expected to be genetically:

options.text: Identical to the zygotic embryo in the same seed
Haploid, since they arise from cells of the female gametophyte
Identical to the mother plant, since they arise from its diploid nucellar cells without fertilisation
Triploid, since they develop alongside the endosperm

solution.explanation: In many Citrus and mango varieties, some nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos. The nucellus is diploid tissue of the ovule, i.e. of the mother sporophyte. Since no meiosis or fertilisation is involved (apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction), the nucellar embryos carry the mother plant's genotype. The zygotic embryo, formed by fusion of egg and male gamete, carries paternal genes too.
steps: Nucellar embryo = copy of the mother plant's genotype
solution.why_others_wrong: The zygotic embryo has a paternal contribution, so it differs; nucellar cells are not part of the haploid female gametophyte; ploidy is not determined by nearness to the endosperm.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', apomixis and polyembryony
solution.final_answer: Option C: Identical to the mother plant, since they arise from its diploid nucellar cells without fertilisation

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A plant of genotype aa (female parent) is pollinated with pollen from a plant of genotype Aa. In one particular seed, the embryo is found to be Aa. Assuming normal double fertilisation, the endosperm of that same seed must be:

options.text: aaa, because the endosperm receives no paternal allele
aaA or aaa with equal probability, because the two male gametes are formed independently
AAa, because the endosperm receives two paternal alleles
aaA, because both male gametes of a pollen grain arise by mitosis from one generative cell and carry the same allele

solution.concept: Genetic identity of the two male gametes
solution.explanation: The embryo Aa received A from the male gamete that fused with the egg (the egg is a). Both male gametes delivered by one pollen tube come from mitotic division of the same generative cell of one pollen grain, so the second male gamete also carries A. It fuses with the two polar nuclei (a + a), giving a triploid endosperm aaA.
steps: Embryo Aa: the male gamete fusing with the egg carried A
Both male gametes of one pollen grain are mitotic products: both A
solution.why_others_wrong: The endosperm does receive one paternal set (triple fusion); the two male gametes are not independent; the endosperm gets two maternal sets (polar nuclei) and only one paternal set.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', double fertilisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: aaA, because both male gametes of a pollen grain arise by mitosis from one generative cell and carry the same allele

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which pair of devices prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy?

options.text: Dioecy, as in papaya, and monoecy, as in castor
Dioecy, as in papaya, and self-incompatibility
Self-incompatibility, and placing the anther and stigma at different positions in the flower
Cleistogamy and monoecy, as in maize

solution.explanation: Monoecy (castor, maize) prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy. Dioecy (papaya) prevents both, since a plant bears flowers of only one sex. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen, from the same flower or from other flowers of the same plant, from fertilising the ovules, so it also blocks both. Placing anther and stigma at different positions acts only within a flower, and cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous.
steps: Self-incompatibility: self-pollen of the same flower or other flowers of the same plant rejected
Monoecy and anther-stigma placement: autogamy only; cleistogamy: ensures autogamy
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong pair contains monoecy, anther-stigma placement or cleistogamy, none of which prevents geitonogamy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', outbreeding devices
solution.final_answer: Option B: Dioecy, as in papaya, and self-incompatibility

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The endosperm that persists in a mature castor seed and the perisperm present in a beet seed differ in ploidy.
Statement II: Both the endosperm and the perisperm are formed as a result of fertilisation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The endosperm develops from the primary endosperm cell formed by triple fusion, so it is triploid (3n); castor is an albuminous seed that keeps part of it. Perisperm, in black pepper and beet, is the residual, persistent nucellus, a diploid (2n) maternal tissue. So they differ in ploidy (Statement I true). Perisperm is a remnant of the nucellus and is not a product of fertilisation (Statement II false).
steps: Statement I true; Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', post-fertilisation: endosperm and seed
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
A fruit contains 30 seeds. Each seed developed from a separate ovule (with a single megaspore mother cell) by normal double fertilisation, and one pollen tube entered each ovule. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At least 30 pollen grains germinated on the stigma.
(b) In all, 60 male gametes were released into the embryo sacs.
(c) At least 30 megaspore mother cells underwent meiosis.
(d) At least 30 pollen mother cells must have undergone meiosis.
(e) The fruit developed from 30 separate ovaries.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only

solution.concept: Counting the events behind seed formation
solution.explanation: (a) True: each ovule received its own pollen tube, so at least 30 pollen grains germinated. (b) True: each pollen tube releases two male gametes into the embryo sac (one for syngamy, one for triple fusion): 30 × 2 = 60. (c) True: each ovule's embryo sac came from a megaspore produced by meiosis of its megaspore mother cell. (d) False: one pollen mother cell gives four pollen grains, so 30 pollen grains need only 8 pollen mother cells (30/4, rounded up). (e) False: the ovules of one ovary develop into the seeds of one fruit.
steps: (a) true: one pollen tube per ovule
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) forget that each pollen mother cell yields four pollen grains; options with (e) confuse ovules (which become seeds) with the ovary (which becomes the fruit); 'b, c and e' also leaves out (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants', pre-fertilisation and double fertilisation
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: To determine the genotype of a tall pea plant, it is crossed with a dwarf (recessive) plant. Crossing an organism showing the dominant phenotype with the recessive parent in this way is called a:

options.text: Back-mutation
Reciprocal cross
Test cross
Dihybrid cross

solution.explanation: NCERT: in a typical test cross, an organism showing a dominant phenotype (whose genotype is to be determined) is crossed with the recessive parent instead of being self-crossed. The progeny ratios then reveal the genotype: all dominant if the plant is homozygous, 1 : 1 if it is heterozygous.
solution.why_others_wrong: A reciprocal cross exchanges the sexes of the two parents; a dihybrid cross involves two characters; 'back-mutation' is not a type of cross.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene: test cross
solution.final_answer: Option C: Test cross

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Mendel published his work on the inheritance of characters in 1865, but it remained unrecognised till 1900.
Statement II: The 'factors' that Mendel proposed are now called genes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: Mendel published his work on inheritance of characters in 1865, but for several reasons it remained unrecognised till 1900, when it was rediscovered (Statement I true). Mendel's 'factors', which are passed down unchanged from parent to offspring through the gametes, are now called genes (Statement II true).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', Mendel's laws of inheritance; chromosomal theory of inheritance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (human cell or individual) with List-II (chromosome complement).

List-I:
A. Ovum of a normal woman
B. Somatic cell of a normal man
C. Somatic cell of a person with Turner's syndrome
D. Somatic cell of a person with Klinefelter's syndrome

List-II:
I. 44 autosomes + XXY
II. 22 autosomes + X
III. 44 autosomes + XO
IV. 44 autosomes + XY

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I
A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III
A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

solution.concept: Chromosome complements in normal and aneuploid humans
solution.explanation: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus the sex chromosomes. A normal man is 44 + XY. A woman is 44 + XX, and meiosis gives every ovum 22 + X. Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one X chromosome (45, with XO), and Klinefelter's syndrome by an additional X chromosome (47, XXY).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse the haploid ovum with a diploid cell, or swap the Turner (XO) and Klinefelter (XXY) karyotypes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex determination; chromosomal disorders
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: When the F1 phenotype does not resemble either of the two parents but is in between the two, the phenomenon is called:

options.text: Co-dominance
Incomplete dominance
Pleiotropy
Polygenic inheritance

solution.explanation: NCERT: in incomplete dominance the F1 has a phenotype that does not resemble either parent and is in between the two, as in snapdragon (pink F1 from red × white). In co-dominance the F1 resembles both parents (blood group AB).
steps: F1 in between both parents → incomplete dominance
solution.why_others_wrong: In co-dominance the F1 resembles both parents; pleiotropy is one gene affecting several traits; polygenic inheritance is one trait controlled by several genes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene: incomplete dominance
solution.final_answer: Option B: Incomplete dominance

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: True-breeding tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) pea plants are crossed, and the F1 plants are self-pollinated. Out of 640 F2 plants, how many are expected to be heterozygous tall (Tt)?

solution.explanation: F1 Tt × Tt gives the F2 genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Heterozygotes are 2/4 = 1/2 of the F2: 640 × 1/2 = 320.
solution.why_others_wrong: 160 is the number of TT (or tt) plants; 480 counts all tall plants (TT + Tt); 213 takes 1/3 instead of 1/2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene
solution.final_answer: Option D: 320

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A plant of genotype AaBb, in which the two genes assort independently, is test-crossed with aabb, and 800 progeny are obtained. How many are expected to be aabb?

solution.explanation: AaBb forms four kinds of gametes, AB, Ab, aB and ab, in equal proportion; aabb gives only ab. So the progeny are AaBb, Aabb, aaBb and aabb in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio, and aabb = 800/4 = 200.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 uses 1/16, the F2 fraction of aabb in a selfed dihybrid; 450 uses 9/16; 400 uses 1/2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of two genes
solution.final_answer: Option A: 200

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (phenomenon) with List-II (NCERT example).

List-I:
A. Incomplete dominance
B. Co-dominance
C. Pleiotropy
D. Polygenic inheritance

List-II:
I. Phenylketonuria
II. Human skin colour
III. Flower colour in snapdragon
IV. ABO blood groups

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II

solution.explanation: Snapdragon flower colour (pink F1) shows incomplete dominance; the ABO blood groups (Iᴬ and Iᴮ both expressed in AB) show co-dominance; phenylketonuria (one gene, several phenotypic effects) is NCERT's example of pleiotropy; human skin colour is its example of polygenic inheritance.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap incomplete dominance with co-dominance, or pleiotropy with polygenic inheritance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene; polygenic inheritance; pleiotropy
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In snapdragon, red (RR) × white (rr) gives pink F1 plants, and the F1 is self-pollinated. What fraction of the F2 plants will breed true (give only their own flower colour) on self-pollination?

options.text: None of them

solution.explanation: Rr × Rr gives 1 RR (red) : 2 Rr (pink) : 1 rr (white). Only homozygotes breed true: red RR and white rr, which together are 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. Pink plants (Rr) segregate again into red, pink and white.
solution.shortcut: With incomplete dominance each phenotype shows its genotype: red and white breed true, pink does not.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 counts only one homozygous class; 3/4 includes pink heterozygotes, which do not breed true; 'none' ignores the homozygous red and white plants.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene: incomplete dominance
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1/2

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Red-green colour blindness is much rarer in females than in males.
Reason (R): A daughter will normally not be colour blind unless her mother is a carrier (or colour blind) and her father is colour blind.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Why colour blindness is rare in women
solution.explanation: The gene for colour blindness is X-linked recessive. A male, with one X, is colour blind whenever his single X carries the allele. A female needs the allele on both X chromosomes, one from each parent: NCERT notes that the daughter will not normally be colour blind unless her mother is a carrier and her father is colour blind. This stringent requirement (R) is why colour blindness is much rarer in females (A).
steps: A: true (about 8% of males, 0.4% of females)
Female must inherit the allele from both parents: R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex-linked inheritance: colour blindness
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A mother has blood group A, and her child has blood group AB. The child's biological father could have blood group:

options.text: AB only
A, B or AB
O or B
B or AB only

solution.explanation: Blood group AB is IᴬIᴮ, one allele from each parent. A group-A mother (IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi) can give only Iᴬ or i, so the child's Iᴮ must have come from the father. Fathers carrying Iᴮ have blood group B (IᴮIᴮ or Iᴮi) or AB (IᴬIᴮ).
steps: Father must carry Iᴮ: group B or AB
solution.why_others_wrong: 'AB only' forgets that a group-B father also carries Iᴮ; a group-A or group-O father has no Iᴮ to give.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene: co-dominance, multiple alleles
solution.final_answer: Option D: B or AB only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Two parents with normal colour vision have a colour-blind son. For their next child, if it is a daughter, what are the probabilities that she is colour blind and that she is a carrier, respectively?

options.text: 0 and 1/2
0 and 1

solution.explanation: The son's X chromosome (carrying the allele) came from his mother, so the normal mother is a carrier (XᶜX). The father is normal (XY) and always gives his normal X to a daughter. A daughter therefore gets the father's normal X plus either the mother's normal X or her X carrying the allele: never colour blind, carrier with probability 1/2.
steps: Mother: carrier (son got the X from her)
Father: normal X to every daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: A daughter cannot be colour blind without receiving an affected X from the father; '1/4 and 1/4' gives fractions of all children, not of daughters; '0 and 1' assumes the mother always passes the affected X.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex-linked inheritance: colour blindness
solution.final_answer: Option C: 0 and 1/2

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about dominance relationships are correct?

(a) In incomplete dominance, the F2 phenotypic ratio is the same as the F2 genotypic ratio.
(b) In co-dominance, the heterozygote expresses the phenotypes of both alleles.
(c) When pink-flowered F1 snapdragons are self-pollinated, about one-fourth of the F2 plants are red-flowered.
(d) In a person of genotype Iᴬi, the alleles Iᴬ and i show co-dominance.
(e) In incomplete dominance the alleles blend permanently, so red flowers are never recovered in the F2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (c), (d) and (e) only

solution.explanation: (a) True: in snapdragon both ratios are 1 : 2 : 1, because each genotype has its own phenotype. (b) True: in co-dominance the F1 resembles both parents; Iᴬ and Iᴮ both express their sugars in group AB. (c) True: RR (red) is 1/4 of the F2. (d) False: Iᴬ is dominant over i; the person is group A. (e) False: the alleles do not blend; red and white reappear in the F2, which is why incomplete dominance does not violate segregation.
steps: (e) false: no blending; parental types reappear
solution.why_others_wrong: Any option with (d) or (e) is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of one gene: incomplete dominance and co-dominance
solution.final_answer: Option B: (a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In humans, in each pregnancy there is always a 50 per cent probability of either a male or a female child.
Statement II: In the XO type of sex determination, as in grasshoppers, the female produces two kinds of eggs, with and without an X chromosome.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Probability of sex in humans; XO type
solution.explanation: NCERT: the human male produces X- and Y-bearing sperm in equal proportion, while all ova carry X, so in each pregnancy there is always a 50% probability of either a male or a female child (Statement I true). In the XO type, all eggs bear an X chromosome besides the autosomes; it is the male (XO) that produces two kinds of sperm, with and without X (Statement II false).
steps: Statement II: false, the XO male (not the female) produces two kinds of gametes
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex determination
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Individuals with Down's syndrome and individuals with Klinefelter's syndrome both have 47 chromosomes.
Reason (R): Both disorders are caused by the gain of a chromosome (aneuploidy): an additional copy of chromosome 21 in Down's syndrome and an additional X chromosome (XXY) in Klinefelter's syndrome.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Normal humans have 46 chromosomes. Down's syndrome is trisomy of chromosome 21 and Klinefelter's syndrome is XXY; in each, one extra chromosome is gained through failure of segregation of chromatids (aneuploidy), giving 47. The gain of one chromosome (R) is exactly why both have 47 chromosomes (A).
steps: R states the cause of A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', chromosomal disorders
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A woman who is a carrier for haemophilia marries a haemophilic man. Among their daughters, what is expected?

options.text: All are carriers and none is haemophilic
All are haemophilic
Half are carriers and half are normal (non-carriers)
Half are haemophilic and half are carriers

solution.explanation: Mother XᴴXʰ, father XʰY. Every daughter receives the father's Xʰ. From the mother she gets Xᴴ or Xʰ with equal probability. So daughters are XᴴXʰ (carriers) or XʰXʰ (haemophilic), 1/2 each. NCERT notes that such haemophilic females are extremely rare, precisely because they need this combination of parents.
steps: Father gives Xʰ to all daughters
Mother gives Xᴴ or Xʰ (1/2 each)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'All carriers' applies when the mother is normal (non-carrier); 'all haemophilic' would need a haemophilic mother; non-carrier daughters are impossible because the father's X always carries the allele.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex-linked inheritance: haemophilia
solution.final_answer: Option D: Half are haemophilic and half are carriers

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a dihybrid is self-pollinated, the F2 always shows the phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Reason (R): Morgan found that when the two genes in a dihybrid cross were situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations was much higher than that of the non-parental type.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A is false: the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio is expected only when the two genes assort independently and show complete dominance; linked genes (as in Morgan's Drosophila crosses) give parental combinations far more often, and incomplete dominance changes the ratio. R is true: it is NCERT's account of Morgan's dihybrid crosses in Drosophila, and it is the reason why A cannot hold in every case.
steps: A: false ('always' fails for linked genes or incomplete dominance)
R: true (Morgan: parental combinations predominate for genes on the same chromosome)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of two genes; linkage and recombination
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When two genes are tightly linked, the recombinant classes in a test cross greatly outnumber the parental classes.
Statement II: In a test cross of a dihybrid AaBb whose two genes assort independently, the four progeny classes are expected in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Statement I is false: tightly linked genes show very low recombination, so the parental classes greatly outnumber the recombinants (Morgan: 1.3% recombination for yellow body and white eye). Statement II is true: an independently assorting dihybrid forms AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes equally, giving 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 with aabb.
steps: Statement I: false, parental types predominate with linkage
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', linkage and recombination
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Suppose a polygenic trait is controlled by three genes A, B and C, and each dominant allele adds an equal amount to the phenotype. A plant AaBbCc is crossed with aabbcc. How many phenotypic classes will the progeny show, and what fraction of the progeny will have the same phenotype as the AaBbCc parent?

options.text: 7 classes; 5/16
4 classes; 1/8
4 classes; 3/8
8 classes; 1/8

solution.concept: Additive polygenes in a test cross
solution.explanation: aabbcc contributes no dominant alleles, so each progeny's number of dominant alleles equals the number it gets from AaBbCc: 0, 1, 2 or 3, with probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8, 1/8. With additive effects, phenotype depends only on this number, so there are 4 classes. The AaBbCc parent has 3 dominant alleles; progeny with 3 (genotype AaBbCc) are 1/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 classes and 5/16 belong to the selfed cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc; 3/8 is the fraction with one (or two) dominant alleles; 8 counts genotypes, not additive phenotypes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', polygenic inheritance
solution.final_answer: Option B: 4 classes; 1/8

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Both parents are unaffected carriers of phenylketonuria, an autosomal recessive disorder. If they have two children, what is the probability that exactly one of the two children is affected?

solution.explanation: Each child of Aa × Aa is affected (aa) with probability 1/4 and unaffected with 3/4, independently. Exactly one affected can happen in two orders (first affected, second not; or the reverse): 2 × (1/4 × 3/4) = 6/16 = 3/8.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 is the probability for one child; 3/16 counts only one birth order; 1/16 is the probability that both children are affected.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', Mendelian disorders: phenylketonuria

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Genes A and B lie on the same chromosome, with 20 per cent recombination between them. A dihybrid that received Ab from one parent and aB from the other is test-crossed with aabb, giving 1000 progeny. How many progeny of genotype AaBb are expected?

solution.concept: Recombinants depend on the parental combination
solution.explanation: The dihybrid's parental (non-recombinant) gametes are Ab and aB; the recombinant gametes are AB and ab. With 20% recombination, AB and ab together make 20% of the gametes, 10% each. AaBb progeny come from AB gametes: 10% of 1000 = 100. (The parental classes Aabb and aaBb are 400 each.)
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 treats AB as a parental gamete, which it would be only if the dihybrid had received AB and ab; 250 assumes independent assortment; 200 takes the whole recombinant fraction for one class.

A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal vision. Their daughters later marry men with normal vision. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) All the daughters of the colour-blind man are carriers.
(b) None of the sons of the colour-blind man is colour blind.
(c) About half of the sons born to his daughters are expected to be colour blind.
(d) His sons can pass the allele for colour blindness to their own sons.
(e) About half of the daughters born to his daughters are expected to be colour blind.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b), (c) and (d) only
(a), (c) and (e) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(b), (d) and (e) only

solution.concept: Criss-cross inheritance of an X-linked trait
solution.explanation: The man (XᶜY) gives Xᶜ to every daughter and Y to every son; the mother gives only normal X. (a) True: daughters are XXᶜ carriers. (b) True: sons are XY, normal. (c) True: a carrier daughter married to a normal man has sons XᶜY or XY, half colour blind. (d) False: his sons are normal and do not carry the allele; in any case a father gives Y, not X, to his sons. (e) False: granddaughters through a carrier daughter and a normal father always get a normal X from the father, so none is colour blind (half are carriers).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) are wrong; 'b, d and e' also leaves out (a) and (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', sex-linked inheritance: colour blindness

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A plant heterozygous for four independently assorting genes (AaBbCcDd) is self-pollinated. What fraction of the progeny will be heterozygous at all four loci?

solution.explanation: For each gene, Aa × Aa gives 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa, so the chance of being heterozygous at one locus is 1/2. The four genes assort independently, so the probabilities multiply: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/256 uses 1/4 per locus (a homozygous class); 81/256 is the fraction showing all four dominant phenotypes; 1/8 stops at three loci.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', inheritance of two genes: law of independent assortment
solution.final_answer: Option D: 1/16

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: A woman with normal phenotype has unaffected parents but a brother with phenylketonuria (an autosomal recessive disorder). She marries a man who is known to be a carrier. What is the probability that their first child will have phenylketonuria?

solution.explanation: The brother is affected (aa), so both unaffected parents are carriers (Aa × Aa). The woman is unaffected, so she is AA or Aa in the ratio 1 : 2, i.e. a carrier with probability 2/3. A child of two carriers is affected with probability 1/4. Overall: 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/4 assumes the woman is certainly a carrier; 1/8 takes her carrier probability as 1/2 (forgetting that she is known to be unaffected); 2/3 is her probability of being a carrier, not the child's risk.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Principles of Inheritance and Variation', Mendelian disorders: phenylketonuria
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1/6

solution.explanation: Number of bp = length / distance per bp = (1.36 × 10⁻³ m) / (0.34 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 4 × 10⁶ bp. (NCERT gives the E. coli genome as 4.6 × 10⁶ bp; the round figure here comes from the given length.)

64 per cent

solution.explanation: In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C (Chargaff). T = 18%, so A = 18% and A + T = 36%. The remaining 64% is G + C, shared equally: G = 32%.

Which of the following statements about the action of the bacterial RNA polymerase during transcription are correct?

(a) It uses nucleoside triphosphates as substrates.
(b) Only a short stretch of RNA remains bound to the enzyme during elongation.
(c) Once the polymerase reaches the terminator region, the nascent RNA falls off, and so does the RNA polymerase.

(a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (c) and (e) only
(b), (c), (d) and (e) only

(a) and (c) only

(a), (b) and (c) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Meselson and Stahl transferred E. coli grown in ¹⁵NH₄Cl into ¹⁴NH₄Cl medium and analysed the DNA after one generation (20 minutes) by CsCl density-gradient centrifugation. If DNA replication had been conservative (both parental strands staying together and both new strands forming a new molecule) instead of semiconservative, what would they have observed after this one generation?

options.text: A single hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) band
Equal amounts of hybrid and light DNA
A single light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N) band
Two bands, one heavy (¹⁵N/¹⁵N) and one light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N), and no hybrid band

solution.concept: Why the Meselson-Stahl result proved semiconservative replication
solution.explanation: Conservative replication would keep the parental ¹⁵N/¹⁵N duplex intact and make an entirely new ¹⁴N/¹⁴N duplex, giving a heavy and a light band after one generation, with no hybrid. What was actually observed after 20 minutes was a single hybrid (intermediate) band, which fits semiconservative replication: each daughter molecule has one old ¹⁵N strand and one new ¹⁴N strand.
steps: Observed: one hybrid band at 20 min → semiconservative
solution.why_others_wrong: A single hybrid band is the actual (semiconservative) result after one generation; equal hybrid and light DNA is the semiconservative result after two generations (40 minutes); a single light band would need all the parental ¹⁵N DNA to disappear.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Molecular Basis of Inheritance', replication: the experimental proof

steps: Population ecology ↔ population genetics and evolution
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT does not single out biochemistry, taxonomy or physiology as the fields that population ecology links ecology to.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations

About 3.4 years

(b) Introducing a predator from its natural habitat may bring it under control.

(a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (c) and (e) only

(b) Reasonable: the cactus was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced. (c) Reasonable: the Abingdon tortoise became extinct within a decade of goats arriving on its island. (d) is the reverse of the truth. questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a population growing logistically according to dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K] with K = 1000, the growth rate dN/dt is greater when N = 500 than when N = 900.
Statement II: In the same population, the per capita growth rate is the same when N = 500 and when N = 900.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Growth rate and per capita rate in logistic growth
solution.explanation: At N = 500: dN/dt = r × 500 × 500/1000 = 250r. At N = 900: dN/dt = r × 900 × 100/1000 = 90r. So Statement I is true. The per capita growth rate, (1/N)(dN/dt) = r(K − N)/K, is 0.5r at N = 500 and only 0.1r at N = 900; it falls as N approaches K, so Statement II is false.
steps: Per capita: 0.5r versus 0.1r → Statement II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', population growth: logistic growth
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Organisms and Populations', populations: population attributes and growth

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Grassland P has a gross primary productivity of 20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, and its plants use 25 per cent of it in respiration. Which ecosystem has more biomass available for consumption by heterotrophs, and by how much?

Q, by 3,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹
P, by 3,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹
P, by 13,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹

solution.concept: Net primary productivity is what heterotrophs can use
solution.explanation: The biomass available to heterotrophs (herbivores and decomposers) is the net primary productivity, NPP = GPP − R. P: 20,000 − 5,000 = 15,000. Q: 30,000 − 18,000 = 12,000. P exceeds Q by 3,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
In a food web, grass is eaten by rabbits and grasshoppers; sparrows eat grass seeds and grasshoppers; frogs eat grasshoppers; snakes eat frogs and rabbits; hawks eat snakes and sparrows. Taking producers as the first trophic level, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The sparrow occupies the second and third trophic levels.
(b) The hawk can occupy the fifth trophic level.
(c) The frog is a primary consumer.
(d) The snake occupies the third and fourth trophic levels.

(a), (b) and (d) only
(b), (d) and (e) only
(a), (b), (c) and (d) only

solution.concept: Organisms at more than one trophic level
solution.explanation: (a) True: eating seeds, the sparrow is a primary consumer (2nd level); eating grasshoppers, a secondary consumer (3rd). (d) True: snake eating rabbit (2nd) is at the 3rd level; snake eating frog (frog eats grasshopper: 3rd) is at the 4th. (b) True: a hawk eating a snake that ate a frog is at the 5th level (it can also be at the 3rd or 4th via sparrows or rabbit-eating snakes). (c) False: the frog eats herbivorous grasshoppers, so it is a secondary consumer (primary carnivore). (e) False: all consumers depend on producers directly or indirectly.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In a grazing food chain, the producers fix 20,000 kJ of energy, and only 10 per cent of the energy is transferred from each trophic level to the next. If the top carnivore of the chain receives 2 kJ, at which trophic level is it (taking producers as the first level)?

options.text: Fifth
Fourth
Sixth
Third

solution.concept: Using the 10 per cent law to count trophic levels
solution.explanation: Energy falls tenfold at each step: 20,000 (1st, producers) → 2,000 (2nd) → 200 (3rd) → 20 (4th) → 2 (5th). So the top carnivore is at the fifth trophic level. This rapid fall is why the number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain is restricted.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fourth' counts the transfers (4) instead of the levels; 'sixth' adds one level too many; 'third' would receive 200 kJ.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow: 10 per cent law
solution.final_answer: Option A: Fifth

Ethical: every species has an intrinsic value. Bioprospecting: exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the narrowly and broadly utilitarian arguments, or the ethical argument with bioprospecting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: why should we conserve biodiversity
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.question_text: The IUCN (2004) puts the number of species described so far at slightly more than 1.5 million. If, as Robert May's estimate implies, only about 22 per cent of all species have been described, the total global species diversity works out to roughly:

options.text: 0.33 million
1.8 million
70 million

solution.explanation: If 1.5 million species are 22 per cent of the total, the total = 1.5/0.22 ≈ 6.8 million, i.e. about 7 million. This matches Robert May's global estimate of species diversity, about 7 million.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Species richness follows log S = log C + Z log A. Take Z = 0.1 for areas within a region and Z = 1.0 for very large areas such as whole continents (both within NCERT's ranges). When the area studied increases tenfold, by about what factor does species richness increase in each case?

options.text: About 1.26 times in both cases
About 1.26 times within a region, but 10 times at the continental scale
10 times within a region, but about 1.26 times at the continental scale
About 1.1 times within a region, but 2 times at the continental scale

solution.explanation: From the equation, S₂/S₁ = (A₂/A₁)^Z. For a tenfold area increase: within a region, 10^0.1 ≈ 1.26; at the continental scale, 10^1.0 = 10. NCERT notes that Z lies between 0.1 and 0.2 within a region but is much steeper (0.6 to 1.2) for very large areas such as entire continents.
solution.why_others_wrong: '1.26 in both' ignores the steeper continental slope; the third option swaps the two cases; 1.1 and 2 come from adding Z to 1 instead of raising 10 to the power Z.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species-area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option B: About 1.26 times within a region, but 10 times at the continental scale
